summaries.example: Imagine studying a school garden. A science class might measure how plants grow and look for patterns that apply to many plants. A history class might tell the special story of one old tree because it matters to the school community. Rickert would say these are different ways of making useful ideas from the same busy world.
summaries.summary: Heinrich Rickert was a German philosopher connected with the Southwestern school of Neo-Kantianism. He asked how knowledge becomes valid and objective. He argued that thinking does not merely copy what our senses give us. Instead, it shapes and selects that material according to concepts and values. Rickert distinguished natural sciences, which usually seek general laws, from historical and cultural sciences, which often study unique events and their connections to shared values. He also developed a broad philosophy about truth, culture, philosophy, reality, and meaning. His work changed over time because he repeatedly revised his major books, but some basic ideas stayed important throughout his career.
key_ideas: Rickert belonged to the Southwestern school of Neo-Kantianism. He wanted philosophy to study the rules that make thinking valid.
He said knowledge is not simply a picture copied from the world. Thinking selects and organizes what we notice.
Natural science usually looks for general laws. History and other cultural studies often focus on meaningful individual events.
Values help explain why some people, events, and objects become important subjects of history.
Rickert thought philosophy should connect different kinds of knowledge and think about the world as a whole.
summaries.why_it_matters: Rickert helps us notice that every subject chooses a way to describe the world. A scientist, historian, artist, and community member may look at the same thing but ask different questions. His ideas can help us think carefully about evidence, fairness, cultural importance, and the difference between finding patterns and understanding unique events.

important_terms.definition: A rule or principle that helps thinking work correctly, even though it is not learned just by observing one event.
The study of how we know things and what makes knowledge trustworthy.
Something people think is important or worthwhile, such as truth, beauty, or fairness.
A way of studying things by looking for broad patterns and laws.
A way of studying something special and one-of-a-kind, especially in history.

questions_to_think_about: When you study a place, what details do you choose to notice, and what do you leave out?
Can the same event be studied both as an example of a general pattern and as a unique story?
What makes something important to a whole community rather than only to one person?
Is knowing something like making a picture, or does it involve organizing and judging?

summaries.example: Consider a revolution. A natural scientist might study general facts about population, disease, or climate that apply across many cases. A historian, by contrast, may investigate this particular revolution as a unique event, asking how its actions and people relate to shared values such as political freedom. The historian need not approve or condemn those values; she can study how the event became value-related and historically significant.
summaries.summary: Heinrich Rickert was a leading figure of Southwestern, or Baden, Neo-Kantianism. His central concern was validity: the principles that make thought, knowledge, science, and cultural judgment objective. Against psychological accounts, he held that valid principles are not just facts about how human minds happen to work. In epistemology, he argued that knowledge cannot be understood as a mental picture of a mind-independent reality. Judgment transforms sensory material into a logically structured claim, and its objectivity ultimately depends on transcendent values, especially truth. In his philosophy of science, Rickert distinguished generalizing concept-formation in the natural sciences from individualizing concept-formation in the historical sciences. History selects unique events through their relation to generally acknowledged cultural values, without reducing historical inquiry to personal approval. His broader philosophy developed an open system of values and a conception of philosophy as a scientific, systematic theory of worldviews. In later writings, he extended this approach into a pluralist ontology and a metaphysics of the unity of reality and value, while denying that metaphysics can be a science in the ordinary sense.
key_ideas: Rickert and the Marburg Neo-Kantians both focused on validity, but they interpreted Kant differently. The Marburg school emphasized the foundations of natural science, while Rickert emphasized culture, values, and the wider system of human faculties.
Rickert rejected a copy theory of knowledge. A judgment does not merely reproduce sensory content; it gives that content a logically valid form and takes a position by affirming or denying it.

His theory of science distinguishes methods rather than simply dividing subjects into nature and mind. Natural sciences generalize, while historical sciences individualize. The same subject matter can be approached by either method.

Historical inquiry is value-related but should not simply impose the historian’s personal evaluations. A historian can study why an event or person mattered in relation to generally acknowledged values without declaring it good or bad.

Rickert’s philosophy of values aimed at an open framework of cultural values, including truth, beauty, morality, happiness, and religious values. He treated philosophy as a systematic attempt to understand the world as a whole.

In his later work, Rickert developed an ontological pluralism. He distinguished sensible being, understandable meaning-configurations, a pre-objective or pro-physical dimension, and supersensible being, while treating metaphysics as symbolic rather than scientific knowledge.
summaries.why_it_matters: Rickert’s work addresses lasting questions about objectivity in science and history. It shows that selecting concepts, methods, and topics is unavoidable, but it does not follow that inquiry is merely subjective. His distinctions help explain why general laws and unique historical narratives are both legitimate forms of knowledge. They also raise difficult questions about whether values can guide inquiry without controlling its conclusions.

important_terms.definition: A school of philosophy that develops Kant’s critical project by investigating the principles that make valid knowledge possible.
A principle that structures valid thought and is not merely a description of how a particular human mind happens to operate.
The philosophical study of the conditions, standards, and objectivity of knowledge.
Rickert’s term for the objectively valid, non-sensible standard that makes true judgment possible; it is not a physical thing.
The method of forming concepts by treating individual events as instances of general laws.
The method of forming concepts so that unique, value-related events or persons can be understood in their individuality.
The study of what can meaningfully be said to be, including different kinds of being rather than only one basic reality.
Rickert’s method of understanding a whole through two mutually exclusive concepts that complement one another.

questions_to_think_about: Does explaining an event through general laws risk losing what makes that event historically distinctive?
Can historians study values objectively without making any value judgments of their own?
If knowledge is not a copy of reality, what makes a judgment true?
Are physical objects, mental states, and meanings different kinds of being, or forms of one kind?
What might be gained, and what might be lost, by organizing philosophy through complementary opposites?

summaries.example: Suppose your town is deciding what to do with an old bridge. An engineer may calculate forces and materials using rules that apply to many bridges. A local historian may study this bridge’s particular role in migrations, celebrations, or conflicts. Neither approach is automatically the only correct one. Each forms concepts for a different purpose, and the historical approach treats the bridge as important because of its connection with shared cultural values.
summaries.summary: Heinrich Rickert was a German philosopher and a major representative of Southwestern Neo-Kantianism. Neo-Kantians asked what makes thinking valid in fields such as science, ethics, art, politics, and history. Rickert argued that these standards are not merely habits inside individual minds. In his theory of knowledge, he rejected the idea that knowing is like making a photograph of reality. Experience supplies material, but judgment selects and organizes it into a meaningful, logically testable form. The objectivity of knowledge is connected not to a separate physical world copied by the mind, but to values that are valid independently of particular acts of thinking. Rickert’s theory of science distinguishes generalizing methods, which seek laws and recurring patterns, from individualizing methods, which aim to understand unique historical events. Historical research is guided by relations to broadly acknowledged cultural values, although it should not become a personal value judgment. Rickert also proposed an open framework of values and described philosophy as a systematic effort to understand the whole world. In his later work, he developed a pluralist account of being that included physical and psychological realities, meanings, and supersensible values.
key_ideas: Rickert led the Southwestern school of Neo-Kantianism, which differed from the Marburg school’s stronger emphasis on natural science and logical construction.
For Rickert, valid knowledge depends on principles that are objective, not merely on psychological habits.
Knowing is not copying. A judgment organizes what is given in experience into a form that can be affirmed or rejected as true or false.
Natural sciences usually generalize. Historical sciences usually individualize, studying events in their unique connections with shared values.
Value-related history is not the same as personal opinion. Historians can investigate the values connected with an object without simply judging those values themselves.
Rickert viewed philosophy as a systematic study of the world as a whole. His later ontology described several kinds of being, including perceivable things and understandable meanings.
summaries.why_it_matters: Rickert’s ideas help explain why different disciplines can study the same world in different but serious ways. They also show why objectivity does not necessarily mean using only numbers or general laws. His account invites us to examine how concepts, purposes, and values shape research while still asking whether conclusions are valid.

important_terms.definition: A movement that reworked Kant’s philosophy by asking which principles make knowledge valid in different areas of thought.
A principle that guides valid thinking and is not simply a report about how people’s minds usually behave.
The study of knowledge, including how a belief or judgment can be objective rather than merely personal.
Something regarded as worthwhile or important, such as truth, beauty, freedom, or community.
Making concepts that emphasize common patterns and laws across many cases.
Making concepts that preserve the special character of a unique person, event, or object.
The study of what kinds of things exist and how they can meaningfully be described.
A method that understands a whole by pairing concepts that oppose but also complete each other.

questions_to_think_about: Why might the same object need both a scientific description and a historical interpretation?
Is it possible to study values without secretly approving or rejecting them?
What is the difference between a mental act of judging and the truth of the judgment?
Do general laws explain everything important about human life?
Can two opposing concepts together give a better picture of a whole than either one alone?
